# A Classification Pipeline

Build a pipeline that predicts a category (e.g., will this incident report
escalate, or which species an observation records) from its features, and judge
it with a confusion matrix and the right metric. A distinct kind of analysis:
predictive modeling with a categorical outcome.

-   Classification predicts a label, not a number.
-   A confusion matrix shows the kinds of errors a classifier makes.
-   Accuracy alone misleads when classes are imbalanced.
-   The right metric depends on the cost of each kind of error.

## A synthetic incident table

-   We predict whether a disaster incident escalates from two features: its
    severity and its kind.
-   The ecology twin predicts species from an observation's mass and length; the
    same code runs with the columns renamed.
-   Start by pinning the seed, then generate rows.

{{< inc classification/classification.py mark=setup >}}

-   `random.seed` makes the generator reproducible: the same seed gives the same
    rows every run, so a colleague can re-run and check the whole pipeline.

{{< inc classification/classification.py mark=generate >}}

-   `escalated` is the label we will predict: 1 means the incident escalates, 0
    means it does not.
-   The chance of escalation rises sharply with severity, and fires escalate
    more often than power outages, so there is a real signal for a model to
    find.
-   The label is imbalanced: most incidents do not escalate.

{{< inc classification/classification.py mark=rate >}}

## Split and fit

-   Fit on one part of the data and evaluate on the rest, so the score reflects
    how the model does on rows it has not seen.
-   The rows are already in random order, so the first 80% and last 20% form a
    fair split.

{{< inc classification/classification.py mark=split >}}

-   Our classifier is a threshold rule: predict escalation when severity is at
    least some cutoff.
-   It is crude but transparent, and a real pipeline often starts with a simple
    rule before reaching for something fancier.

{{< inc classification/classification.py mark=predict >}}

-   To fit the rule, try each cutoff on the training data and keep the one that
    best balances precision and recall.
-   First we need to count the four kinds of outcomes, and turn those counts
    into scores.

{{< inc classification/classification.py mark=confusion >}}

-   A true positive is an escalation we caught; a true negative is a
    non-escalation we correctly ignored.
-   A false positive is a false alarm; a false negative is an escalation we
    missed.
-   Precision is the fraction of our alarms that were real; recall is the
    fraction of real escalations we caught.
-   F1 is their harmonic mean, a single number that rewards both at once.

{{< inc classification/classification.py mark=fit_threshold >}}

## Predict and evaluate

-   Apply the chosen threshold to the test data, which the fit never saw.

{{< inc classification/classification.py mark=evaluate >}}

-   The matrix has four cells: true negatives top left, false positives top
    right, false negatives bottom left, true positives bottom right.
-   The diagonal is correct answers; the off-diagonal is two different kinds of
    mistake.

{{< inc classification/classification.py mark=metrics >}}

## Why accuracy alone misleads

-   Accuracy is the fraction of rows we got right, but on imbalanced data a
    trivial rule can score well.
-   A classifier that always says "no escalation" gets every non-escalation
    right and only misses the rare escalations.

{{< inc classification/classification.py mark=baseline >}}

-   With about a third of incidents escalating, "always no" is right roughly
    two times in three, yet it catches none of the escalations.
-   Its accuracy is just the share of the majority class, which is why the
    number alone is deceptive.
-   Accuracy hides that failure; recall exposes it.
-   Which metric matters depends on the cost of each kind of error.
-   If a missed escalation costs lives, prefer high recall: we would rather send
    some false alarms than miss one real escalation.
-   If every alarm sends a crew and crews are scarce, prefer high precision: we
    would rather miss an occasional escalation than waste a crew.
-   There is no single best metric; there is a metric that matches the decision
    the model feeds.

-   The ecology twin is the same shape: predict `species` from `mass_g` and
    `length_mm`, and judge the result with the same confusion matrix.
-   Rename the label, swap the feature columns, and the pipeline runs unchanged.
